Description

Glutamate released from nociceptor central terminals activates AMPA receptors, whose Na+ current depolarises dorsal horn neurons and drives firing. Depolarisation relieves the Mg2+ block of NMDA receptors, and their Ca2+ influx, joined in inflammation by GluA2-lacking AMPA receptors, starts the kinase signalling of central sensitisation. Spinal neurons in rat models of knee OA respond more strongly to joint stimuli, and patients with painful knee OA show signs of central sensitisation.

Colour

Proteins and metabolites are coloured by their contribution to pain: red for those that raise it (they excite or sensitise nociceptive neurons, or drive the inflammation that does), blue for those that relieve it, and olive for the shared signalling machinery (G proteins, RGS, adenylate cyclase, phospholipases, kinases, adaptors, second messengers, ions and nucleotides), whose effect is set by the receptor upstream. Drugs are yellow and classes of molecules white. Each molecule is coloured by its role in this block, so the same molecule can be red in one block and blue in another.

Glutamate and its AMPA and NMDA receptors are red as the route of every nociceptive signal from the nociceptor to the dorsal horn neuron. What turns this normal transmission into pain hypersensitivity, central sensitisation, is the change in the density, nature and properties of the glutamate receptors (Latremoliere 2009). The red marks the route, not only that gain.
